Here, where the old world still held its breath, the sun moved slowly across the sky, casting long shadows over the thatched roofs and ivy-clad walls. It was a place where time had forgotten to march forward, where the past was not just remembered but lived in the bones of the people who called this narrow valley home.

Evelyn Harrow had always been a stranger to the rhythm of the village. With her ink-stained fingers and eyes that held the weight of a thousand stories, she was an outsider—both by birth and by choice. She had come seeking answers, not in the dusty tomes of the local library, but in the quiet murmurs of the wind that passed through the trees at dawn. The village had little to offer her except the wary glances of its inhabitants and the hushed warnings of the elders. But Evelyn did not seek their approval. She sought truth, and truth, in Blackthorn Hollow, was a dangerous thing.

It was on the third evening of her stay that she found him—a man whose presence seemed to bend the very light around him. His name was Dain, and he was a painter, though the villagers whispered that his brush captured more than mere color. They said he saw the soul of the world in every stroke, and that his art was as much a curse as it was a gift. And when Evelyn met his gaze, she felt as though the world itself had paused to listen.
